Notes from Thomas

“YOU CAN’T TAKE IT WITH YOU” artwork/poster ideas…

The overall take-away here is that this is a wacky family in an ordinary upscale neighborhood on the Upper West Side of NYC that plays by their own rules. Enjoy life NOW! You can’t take it with you when you die, so squeeze all you can out of this life! 

Grandpa (the focal character) doesn’t believe in paying income tax and the IRS is constantly on his case, but he doesn’t care. He was a rich man — hence the brownstone — who one day just walked away from his job so he could enjoy life. This attitude has passed down to his daughter (and her husband) and her children, as well — all of whom live in one big house together. They also take in “stray” people and are accepting of everyone. When the one “normal” granddaughter falls in love with a businessman, his parents get drawn into this hilarious oddity, showing that maybe the unconventional way IS the better way. 

	⁃	A row of Upper West Side brownstones with one obviously belonging to a wacky family — perhaps fireworks coming out of windows or roof, printed flyers scattered on the front step, an IRS letter tacked to the door, etc.

	⁃	A 1930s poster “feel” with some elements of what clutters this ordinary home’s living room — a small manual printing press, a terrarium of snakes, an easel with a canvas on it and paint supplies, an old typewriter with stacks of manuscripts, a xylophone, fireworks, a summons from the IRS, etc.

	⁃	Perhaps some character drawings of a few of the more outlandish characters — Essie (a really in-talented ballerina wannabe), Mr. Kohlinkhov (a Russian ballet teacher in the look of a friendly Rasputin), the Grand Duchess Olga Katryna (older Russian aristocrat in full royal regalia and fur stole, but somewhat worse-for-wear), Mr. DePinna (in his toga posed as a discus thrower for a painting)…I have saved a few posters showing things like that. I love the line-drawings (aka Hirschfeld) because it’s not as specific (gives me more casting freedom than specific drawings).

I really like the most recent Broadway one, but feel free to play around with them all! The only other text (besides Apex, Hart and Kaufman, etc. and my name as director) other than the title I WOULD like is the words “Pulitzer Prize winning play” or something like that, specifying it’s a Pulitzer winner.

I love that this has the generic “normal” couple — who the show revolves around — along with several of those other things: IRS note, the leaflets spilling, the fireworks, the NYC skyline in the distance (Chrysler Building and Empire State Building were only a few years old) with brownstones in front. It even has a xylophone and a kitten (not sure if I’m gonna do live kittens 

Director’s Notes

(copied from email from Mary Thompson to Kevin)

Below I've pasted each director's vision for their productions. Chloe will soon send show summaries. Betty Clark didn't give you much to work with here. There was a movie of Rabbit Hole with Nicole Kidman that might be instructive.

We will know in the next couple of weeks which of the first two listed is "the one."

Also, please note spelling of "Theatre" for our proper name. Otherwise, we follow AP style and spell it theater. 

Very excited to get going on this. 

The Cake
I laughed out loud when I read The Cake by Bekah Brunstetter. And then I cried. And then I laughed again. There is a great deal of humour in The Cake. Della, the main character in the show has a quiet but determined character and yet she is touchingly sweet in her lack of awareness. This creates a relatable, vulnerable character that I think our audiences will fall in love with. Her naive reactions, when the modern world and its values invade her comfortable life, are alternately hilarious and heartbreaking.

In these troubled times, when people are ruled by division of philosophy and morals, I see The Cake as a way of bringing people together. Della is ultra conservative, but she is a woman with a big heart, an eternal optimist who makes the best of the cards he has been dealt. She is a dreamer who has bought into the idea that if she is ‘good’ and follows the rules, all will go well in her life. Of course all has not gone well, but she copes. And then she is faced with a decision that upends all her beliefs and wishes. I see this play as a way for us all to think about the people that we might dismiss from our lives because they have different beliefs. It is a vehicle for showing that ‘the other’ is struggling too. It is a play about love, ethics and how we all make our decisions. One of the criteria I have for choosing a play, right or wrong, is whether the characters are lovable; will the audiences care about them and their problems? It will not be a difficult task to make Della, indeed all the characters in The Cake, lovable. They just are. Even Tim, with his ultra conservative attitude to life, marriage, love and sex, has a kind heart and solid reasons for his behavior. Each character in the play has a wonderful arc and I think our audiences will love going on the journey with them.

I also hope to manage some kind of collaboration with a local cake shop so that we may have beautiful cakes for sale in the lobby each evening and possibly more talk backs with the actors than usual. I imagine going into the lobby after the show and actors talking with audience members while they eat their delicious cake!

Rabbit Hole
Rabbit Hole’s theme is about with how people in this case parents deal with the loss of their child. I feel the main purpose of theater is to mirror society and the human spirit Rabbit Hole is very well written to touch any audience emotionally.  Though the play’s subject is sad and painful, there is humor and somewhat complicated family relationships all making the play well rounded and relevant for any audience.

Company
The central theme of Company is the challenge of maintaining relationships in a society that is becoming increasingly depersonalized. In a series of playlets by George Furth, Company explores the complications of marriage, friendship, love, isolation and loneliness in 1970’s New York City.  Company was one of the first “concept” musicals.

It has a story, but doesn’t have a chronological linear plot.  Rather than serving to advance the plot, the songs comment on the action and analyze it as it happens.  The sets provide atmosphere rather than physical location.

Even though Company is a period piece, set in 1970, its exploration of the complications of relationships in a fast-paced environment is a contemporary theme.  We face today the consequences of depersonalization in our lives as we increasingly communicate solely by social media and technology. 

2020 will be the 50th anniversary of Company’s New York premier in 1970.  In 1971 Company scored 15 nominations for Tony Awards, then a record, and won 7 awards, Best Musical, Best Music, Best Lyrics, Best Book, Best Scene Design, Best Director and Best Producer.  Apex has not produced Company since its very successful production in 1978.  

Company is sophisticated, witty and urban with a fabulous book and score, arguably one of Sondheim’s very best musicals.   

She Kills Monsters - See attached for some thoughts about the "tone" of the costume design
(Please, make sure you are considering the Young Adventurers version of this play. The there is big distinction between the two plays the Young Adventurers version is a story about two sisters and their relationship. The other version of the play is a story about the journey and exploration of sexual identity. VERY DIFFERENT PLAYS.)
 
She Kills Monsters: Young Adventurers offers self-awareness as an action adventure with some kick-ass escapism. We envision a fun and funny action-packed quest with both surprising and comic special effects to provide audiences a thrilling good time. We anticipate that in 2020 with tensions in the world, audiences will really enjoy a good escape into an evening of adventure.

Key themes for She Kills Monsters: Young Adventurers include:
slaying the very real monsters of real life; in this case the guilt of things not noticed and faced,
taking those close to you for granted and learning about their passions and secrets too late,
the fierce bonds of sisterhood, and
facing and moving through perceptions and prejudices.
The themes are all relevant for today’s audiences “monsters” are everywhere both of our own creation and those we see in others. Old and young audience members can recognize the guilt of things ignored or assumed in those close to us, as well as the journey that is required to face and take-down the monsters in our lives.  This play invites audience members to relate to the facing of fears and prejudices in a fun kick-ass, D&amp;D, kind of way.
 
She Kills Monsters: Young Adventurers is relevant to today’s audiences because it is told in a very contemporary style with the focus of the play on the relationship between the two sisters and that the younger sister is a girl geek and a Dungeon Master. 

The Fantasticks
The foremost theme is the timeless lesson of growing up and the journey from innocence to knowledge/awareness…the loss of childhood innocence and the rocky travels entering into adulthood.

NOBODY escapes this journey! It is life. Young people will see themselves in Matt and Louisa’s struggle for independence and the autonomy to pursue their dreams and older people will recognize the struggle as one they also endured.

2020 will be the the 60th anniversary of the opening of The Fantasticks Off-Broadway where it ran for 42 years. It is a small show (cast of 8). The simple, basic look that fits perfectly into the Apex setting.

It is my number one, all time, FAVORITE musical. It has my heart. I want to direct it in the style in which it was originally created…no glitz or sparkles…just a platform, a trunk and the original Fantasticks curtain that Daniel Ramirez will create.…very improvisational/street theater style in which it was created, in its’ specific simplicity.  

Ripcord
Ripcord is a play about two women who have been assigned to share a room at the Bristol Place Senior Living Facility, a place that is often the last home for many people at their age. For the last four years, Abby, a cantankerous and private woman, has chased away all previous roommates so she can have a private room, and intends to do the same with her new roommate. But Marilyn, a perky and optimistic woman, has no intention of leaving. She likes the light coming through the windows and the view of the park. So they make a bet that if Abby can make Marilyn angry, Marilyn will move out. And if Marilyn can scare Abby, then Marilyn will get the bed by the window. The two women then begin to live life to the fullest, pulling one prank after another on each other in an attempt to win the bet. Marilyn’s daughter and son-in-law visit, and end up getting involved in the pranks. Abby reconnects with her son in a heart wrenching reunion. Scotty, the caregiver from Bristol Place, invites Abby and Marilyn to come see him at his annual haunted house. Along the way, Abby and Marilyn find out a lot about each other, and about themselves.

Past survey and past practice has shown that the audiences at Apex Theatre enjoy a good laugh and a heartwarming story. Ripcord has both of these factors built in. Many of Apex’s audience members are older, or have aging parents. Whether an aging person or the child of an aging person, or somebody who just wants a good laugh and a touching story, audiences will be able to relate to the characters in Ripcord and the emotions they all face. The show is entertaining, but also very thoughtful.

Ripcord may not be a well recognized name, but the author is a well-known author with many awards to his name. This show brings warmth and laughter to all ages because it’s very human. The show is family friendly for older children (there are a few swear words and scary characters in the haunted house), and will leave new audience members wanting to return for more shows like this one. This play offers the opportunity for two older women, which, as actors age, are harder to find. There are also roles for one female and two male characters in the mid 20s to 30s.    

Shrek
On the surface SHREK can seem like a simple fairytale comedy, but the show has true heart. It tackles important topic such as:
Beauty – what is it, and who decides what beautiful is? How do we learn to accept and embrace our inner beauty if the outside world finds us to be hideous?
Loneliness &amp; friendship – Shrek prefers to be alone because he has never truly experienced what friendship actually is. He starts off angry and annoyed at everyone; through his journey to rid his swamp of the fairytale creatures he develops a sweet friendship with Donkey. Both of the characters deal with loneliness for different reasons and both find solace in one another, creating a meaningful friendship along the way.
Love – Shrek and Fiona seem to be polar opposites when they first meet. Shrek is described as an onion, with layered feelings. Fiona is an embolden “princess” with strong opinions but a deep secret, forcing her to keep any potential suitors at an arms length. Each of them learns to trust the other through honesty and embracing who they are, eventually growing to loving one another. The beautiful princess is able to see the ugly Ogre for who he truly is. 
Embrace who you are – the Fairy tale creatures are banished from Duloc and made to feel inferior by Lord Farquaad. They have a rousing song called “Freak Flag” which speaks to embracing who you really are and not caring what others think of you as long as you are true to yourself.    
Our audiences can relate the themes presented in Shrek as they affect most people in someway or another, either personally or through someone they know. I don’t know anyone who hasn’t struggled with self-image issues through middle school and high school at some point. Shrek presents a unique vulnerability to be strong on the outside but deeply want to connect with people while feeling isolated and alone. Further I think Shrek could be particularly relevant to our current socio-political environment. One in which we are all striving for equality amongst all people, gender, races, religions etc.

Something Rotten!
Concept Sketches
Andrew Davis

I started with quick doodles combining the Hamlet skull with a cracked egg, either cracked on top of the skull or the skull sitting in the cracked yolk like the egg had been dropped.

&lt;image attachment&gt;
(Quick doodles of a skull combined with a cracked egg)

This turned into seeing if I could get the yolk itself to read as a skull, which is a fun idea but I’m not sure if it conveys the Hamlet scene.
&lt;image attachment&gt;
(Sketch of an egg yolk shaped like a skull)

I actually like the first drawing of the regular egg yolk the most, but it’s missing the second half of the idea. I chose purple as the background for these sketches because it’s a royal / magical color appropriate for the Shakespearean setting. It’s also the complementary color of yellow so it gives a strong contrast with the yolk.
My main concern at this point was that a skull on its own might not convey “Hamlet.” The iconic image of the play is Hamlet talking to Yorick’s skull and many Hamlet posters include a hand or figure holding the skull. After looking at some references and trying to find an egg-y spin on them, I had the idea to replace the skull in the hand with an egg:

&lt;image attachment&gt;
(Sketches of a hand holding an egg, one with yolk dribbling out)

(These hands look a little strange, I would have to find a better pose for this if we went with this.) I didn’t think these read as “Hamlet” very much either. The egg might need something else like a small crown or jester hat. I liked the yolk dribbling out of the egg here in the last one.

I felt like I was getting further away from the original idea and comedic tone. The splatted / cracked egg felt like it was important to include, not just a plain egg. I also wanted the poster to instantly read as a goofy comedy full of Shakespeare references. I went back to the first doodle of the egg crunched on top of a skull, but brought in the hand holding the skull for more context.

&lt;image attachment&gt;
(Sketch of a hand holding a skull topped with a cracked egg)

I wanted the arm to be wearing something appropriate for the time period. This felt like a solid direction, mixing Hamlet and the egg into something that was funny and made sense right away.

After trying out different fonts and layouts I ended up with this:

&lt;image attachment&gt;
(Final poster design concept, previous illustration with text and illustration)

This design combined the elements I was looking for and was visually interesting. I think the concept gets across immediately, which was an issue with some of the earlier sketches.

My potential issues with this idea:
It’s not obvious that the play is a musical, a tagline might fix this.
I’m always iffy about including skin tones on the posters since we want it to be inclusive. Solutions could be having the hand wear a glove, or have no skin tone at all.

I think this would be a good direction to go for the final concept art for the reveal, what do you think? If any of the other sketches resonated with you I can spend some time with them and see where they go. We’ve got about two weeks until I need to land on a final idea and tidy it up for the concept art reveal.

Please let me know what you think! This play was very fun to get to know, I’ve been listening to the soundtrack all week. Thanks!

Andrew Davis &lt;andrewndav@email.com&gt;

Task:


Based on the email thread between Andrew and James, reconstruct the step-by-step evolution of the 'Something Rotten!' poster design from the initial doodles to the final approved concept. For each iteration, explain exactly what feedback was given, who gave it, and how the artist interpreted and adapted that feedback in the next version. Present this in chronological order.

Based on the email thread between Andrew Davis and James Wilson, the evolution of the 'Something Rotten!' poster design occurred in the following steps:

**Step 1: Initial Concept Sketches (Referenced, not shown)**
*   **Artist's Action:** Andrew Davis created initial concept sketches. Based on his descriptions in a separate document, these included doodles of a Hamlet skull combined with a cracked egg (either the egg cracked on top of the skull, or the skull sitting in the cracked yolk). He also explored the idea of the yolk itself being shaped like a skull. He considered adding a hand holding the skull, replacing Yorick's skull with an egg.
*   **Feedback:** None recorded in the email thread for these initial ideas. They were sent to director James Wilson for review.

**Step 2: First Directed Iteration (June 25, 2025)**
*   **Feedback Given:** James Wilson responded to an initial sketch (sent by Andrew on June 25 at 6:25 PM). He requested a change: "Could we make it more cartoony and have the full egg broken with shells on the side and the skull in the middle of the yolk?" (Given by James Wilson).
*   **Artist's Interpretation:** Andrew Davis received this feedback and began working on a new version that incorporated a broken egg with shells and a skull positioned within the yolk.

**Step 3: Second Iteration - Two New Sketches (June 30, 2025, 5:51 PM)**
*   **Artist's Action:** Andrew Davis sent two new sketches to James Wilson.
    1.  **Sketch 1 ("Egg Sketch"):** An image of an egg yolk shaped like a skull. Andrew noted he liked an earlier version of a regular egg yolk but felt it was incomplete.
    2.  **Sketch 2 ("Hand Sketch"):** Sketches of a hand holding an egg. One version showed a yolk dribbling out. Andrew mentioned he was drawn to an earlier idea of a hand holding a skull topped with a cracked egg, which he felt mixed Hamlet and the egg in a funny way.
*   **Interpretation of Feedback:** Andrew was interpreting James's previous direction by experimenting with the skull-and-yolk concept in different ways—both integrating the skull into the yolk's shape and depicting it alongside an egg held in a hand.

**Step 4: Clarification and Refinement Request (June 30, 2025, 6:51 PM)**
*   **Feedback Given:** James Wilson reviewed the two new sketches. He stated, "I like the first one but I’d like the skull to actually IN the yolk." (Given by James Wilson). He was referring to the "Hand Sketch" (the first one he saw in the email) but wanted a different composition where the skull was inside the yolk, not just on top or alongside it.
*   **Artist's Action:** Andrew Davis was confused by the phrasing and sought clarification.

**Step 5: Artist Seeks Clarification (July 1, 2025, 4:00 PM)**
*   **Artist's Action:** Andrew Davis asked for clarification: "By inside the yolk, are you meaning more like the skull has squished / splatted the yolk instead of sitting on top of it, or literally inside of the yolk like a bug trapped in amber?" He promised to send a new version once he understood the intent.

**Step 6: Radical Pivot in Concept (July 1, 2025, 7:30 PM)**
*   **Feedback Given:** James Wilson abandoned the previous line of inquiry and proposed a completely new concept. He suggested: "How about a 'sexy' shakespeare holding a skull up with the cracked egg and yolk dripping down the skull with a odd or horrified or disgusted look." (Given by James Wilson).
*   **Artist's Interpretation:** Andrew Davis received this new directive, which shifted the focus from a symbolic combination of skull and egg to a more literal and thematic scene involving a character.

**Step 7: Execution of the "Sexy Shakespeare" Concept (July 18, 2025, 7:41 AM)**
*   **Artist's Action:** Andrew Davis sent an updated sketch titled "Something Rotten Concept Art.png." This sketch depicted the new idea: a "sexy Shakespeare" (inspired by Christian Bale and historical illustrations) holding a skull, with a cracked egg and dripping yolk incorporated into the image.
*   **Interpretation of Feedback:** Andrew directly implemented James's latest feedback, creating a character-focused design that merged the required elements in a new way.

**Step 8: Final Approval (July 18, 2025, 7:56 AM)**
*   **Feedback Given:** James Wilson reviewed the "sexy Shakespeare" sketch and approved it. He simply stated, "This is approved." (Given by James Wilson).
*   **Outcome:** The design was finalized. The email chain ends with this approval.
